Message passing and graph neural network layers

Source: vignettes/message-passing.Rmd
message-passing.Rmd
library(graphlearnR)
library(torch)
r_vec <- function(t) as.numeric(as.array(t))

A graph neural network layer updates each node from messages sent along its incoming edges. For node i with incoming neighbors \mathcal{N}(i),

h_i' = \gamma\left(h_i,\ \bigoplus_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \phi(h_i, h_j, e_{ji})\right),

where \phi builds a message, \bigoplus is a permutation invariant aggregation such as sum, mean, or max, and \gamma updates the node. This article shows the pieces graphlearnR uses to compute this and how the built in layers fit the pattern.

Scatter aggregation

Aggregation is a scatter: row k of a message matrix is added (or averaged, or maximized) into row index[k] of the output. Rows that receive nothing are zero.

msg <- torch_tensor(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), ncol = 1))
index <- c(1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 4L)
cbind(sum = r_vec(scatter_sum(msg, index, 4)),
      mean = r_vec(scatter_mean(msg, index, 4)),
      max = r_vec(scatter_max(msg, index, 4)),
      count = r_vec(scatter_count(index, 4)))
#>      sum mean max count
#> [1,]   3  1.5   2     2
#> [2,]  12  4.0   5     3
#> [3,]   0  0.0   0     0
#> [4,]   6  6.0   6     1

Node 3 receives no messages, so every aggregation returns 0 for it rather than a missing value or negative infinity. scatter_softmax() normalizes scores within each group, which attention layers use.

r_vec(scatter_softmax(msg, index, 4))
#> [1] 0.26894143 0.73105860 0.09003057 0.24472848 0.66524094 1.00000000

All of these are vectorized torch operations, so they run on the GPU and are differentiable.

The general operator

message_passing() implements the equation above. By default the message is the source features, optionally scaled by edge_weight.

x <- torch_tensor(matrix(c(1, 10, 100), ncol = 1))
ei <- torch_tensor(rbind(c(1, 2, 3), c(3, 3, 1)), dtype = torch_long())
r_vec(message_passing(x, ei, aggr = "sum"))
#> [1] 100   0  11
r_vec(message_passing(x, ei, aggr = "mean"))
#> [1] 100.0   0.0   5.5

Node 3 receives from nodes 1 and 2, node 1 from node 3, and node 2 from no one.

A custom message function is called with named arguments x_j (source features), x_i (target features), edge_attr, edge_weight, index (the target of each edge), and num_nodes, one row per edge. Accept the ones you need and ... for the rest. Here is a message that is the difference between source and target, the core of EdgeConv:

diff_msg <- function(x_j, x_i, ...) x_j - x_i
r_vec(message_passing(x, ei, message = diff_msg, aggr = "max"))
#> [1]  99   0 -90

Writing a layer

A layer is a torch nn_module whose forward() calls message_passing(). This one implements a mean aggregator with separate weights for the node and its neighbors:

my_conv <- nn_module(
  initialize = function(in_features, out_features) {
    self$lin_self <- nn_linear(in_features, out_features)
    self$lin_nbr <- nn_linear(in_features, out_features, bias = FALSE)
  },
  forward = function(x, edge_index) {
    agg <- message_passing(x, edge_index, aggr = "mean")
    self$lin_self(x) + self$lin_nbr(agg)
  }
)

g <- dataset_karate()
tt <- graph_tensors(g)
torch_manual_seed(1)
layer <- my_conv(34, 4)
dim(layer(tt$x, tt$edge_index))
#> [1] 34  4

That is the GraphSAGE update, which graphlearnR also provides as sage_conv().

Built in layers

layer update edge input
sage_conv() W_1 h_i + W_2 \operatorname{mean}_{j} h_j none
gcn_conv() \sum_j \frac{1}{\sqrt{\hat d_i \hat d_j}} W h_j with self loops weights
graph_conv() W_1 h_i + W_2 \sum_j w_{ji} h_j weights
gin_conv() \operatorname{MLP}((1 + \epsilon) h_i + \sum_j h_j) optional features (GINE)
gat_conv() attention weighted sum, multiple heads optional features
gatv2_conv() GATv2 dynamic attention optional features
transformer_conv() scaled dot product attention over neighbors optional features
nn_conv() W_1 h_i + \sum_j \Theta(e_{ji}) h_j (edge conditioned) features, required
rgcn_conv() W_0 h_i + \sum_r \operatorname{mean}_{j \in \mathcal{N}_r(i)} W_r h_j relation type, required

Every layer takes (x, edge_index, ...) and returns new node features.

torch_manual_seed(2)
layers <- list(
  sage = sage_conv(34, 8),
  gcn = gcn_conv(34, 8),
  gin = gin_conv(graph_mlp(c(34, 16, 8))),
  gat = gat_conv(34, 4, heads = 2),
  transformer = transformer_conv(34, 4, heads = 2)
)
sapply(layers, function(l) dim(l(tt$x, tt$edge_index)))
#>      sage gcn gin gat transformer
#> [1,]   34  34  34  34          34
#> [2,]    8   8   8   8           8

Attention layers keep the coefficients of their last forward pass. Within each target node they sum to one.

gat <- layers$gat
invisible(gat(tt$x, tt$edge_index))
alpha <- as.array(gat$last_attention$alpha)
dst <- as.array(gat$last_attention$edge_index)[2, ]
head(rowsum(alpha, dst))
#>   [,1] [,2]
#> 1    1    1
#> 2    1    1
#> 3    1    1
#> 4    1    1
#> 5    1    1
#> 6    1    1

Bipartite input

Most layers also accept a pair list(x_src, x_dst) when sources and targets are different node sets with different feature sizes. Give the input size as a pair too. Heterogeneous models are built on this.

xs <- torch_randn(5, 3)
xd <- torch_randn(2, 7)
bip <- torch_tensor(rbind(c(1, 2, 5), c(1, 2, 2)), dtype = torch_long())
dim(sage_conv(c(3, 7), 4)(list(xs, xd), bip))
#> [1] 2 4

Edge features and relations 

torch_manual_seed(3)
ge <- dataset_karate()
ge$edge_attr <- matrix(runif(num_edges(ge) * 2), ncol = 2)
ge$edge_type <- sample(1:3, num_edges(ge), replace = TRUE)
te <- graph_tensors(ge)
dim(nn_conv(34, 8, edge_dim = 2)(te$x, te$edge_index, edge_attr = te$edge_attr))
#> [1] 34  8
dim(rgcn_conv(34, 8, num_relations = 3, num_bases = 2)(te$x, te$edge_index,
                                                     edge_type = te$edge_type))
#> [1] 34  8

How the layers are tested

The test suite checks every layer for properties that must hold whatever the weights are:

  • Permutation equivariance. Relabeling the nodes relabels the output in the same way.
  • Agreement with a reference formula. GCN is compared with the dense \hat D^{-1/2} \hat A \hat D^{-1/2} X W, GraphSAGE and GIN with explicit neighbor loops, and RGCN with per relation means.
  • Gradients. Input gradients match central finite differences in double precision, and parameter gradients of GCN match the analytic formula.

Here is the equivariance check for GraphSAGE:

torch_manual_seed(4)
layer <- sage_conv(34, 4)
perm <- sample.int(34)
inv <- order(perm)
gp <- g
gp$x <- g$x[perm, ]
gp$edge_index <- matrix(inv[g$edge_index], nrow = 2)
out <- as.array(layer(tt$x, tt$edge_index))
out_p <- as.array(layer(graph_tensors(gp)$x, graph_tensors(gp)$edge_index))
max(abs(out_p - out[perm, ]))
#> [1] 1.490116e-08

Pooling

Graph level models reduce node features to one vector per graph. global_add_pool(), global_mean_pool(), and global_max_pool() take the batch vector; global_attention_pool() learns a gate; topk_pool() keeps the highest scoring fraction of nodes in each graph.

b <- graph_batch(dataset_synthetic_graphs(4, seed = 1))
tb <- graph_tensors(b)
as.array(global_mean_pool(tb$x, b$batch))
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]    1
#> [2,]    1
#> [3,]    1
#> [4,]    1

Continuous depth: graph neural ODEs

Stacking L diffusion layers discretizes a continuous process. GRAND (Chamberlain et al. 2021) makes this explicit: features evolve by \frac{dX}{dt} = (A - I) X, with A the GCN propagation matrix or an attention matrix computed from the input. graph_ode_block() integrates this from 0 to t_end with a fixed number of Runge-Kutta or Euler steps inside the torch graph, so the block trains like any other layer.

g_ode <- split_nodes(dataset_sbm(c(50, 50), seed = 5), seed = 5)
torch_manual_seed(1)
ode <- graph_ode_model(ncol(g_ode$x), hidden_dim = 16, output_dim = 2,
                       diffusion = "attention", t_end = 2, steps = 4)
fit_ode <- train_graph_model(ode, g_ode, "node_classification", epochs = 60, seed = 1)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_ode, g_ode)
#>              metric        value
#> 1          accuracy 1.000000e+00
#> 2 balanced_accuracy 1.000000e+00
#> 3   precision_macro 1.000000e+00
#> 4      recall_macro 1.000000e+00
#> 5          f1_macro 1.000000e+00
#> 6               ece 1.756549e-05
#> 7             brier 2.002353e-09
#> 8           roc_auc 1.000000e+00

The tests compare the block with the closed form solution e^{t(A - I)} X_0 for the GCN operator, and check that constant features are a fixed point of the attention operator. This is a fixed step discretization, not an adaptive ODE solver; for simulating graph dynamics with error control, use graph_diffusion(), which calls modelcompR (see the ecosystem article).
